artists.summary: Steve Albini was a Chicago musician and recording engineer who made raw, live-sounding records for Pixies, Nirvana, PJ Harvey and many others. He led Big Black and Shellac and rejected producer royalties on principle.
know: He preferred a "recorded by" credit to "produced by" and charged a flat fee rather than royalties.
He built and ran Electrical Audio, a studio in Chicago.
He led the bands Big Black and Shellac.

influencedBy.why: The Stooges' raw, loud sound is a model for his recording philosophy.
Albini has named Wire as a key influence on his playing and attitude.
Gang of Four's sharp, scratchy guitar shaped Big Black's sound.
The Birthday Party's abrasive post-punk was a touchstone.
Pere Ubu's noisy, art-damaged rock fed his aesthetic.
The Ramones were his entry point into punk.

cousins.why: Same stripped-back philosophy of capturing a band's raw sound.
Both prized raw, live energy over studio polish.

artists.name: Butch Vig
artists.summary: Butch Vig is a producer and drummer who made Nirvana's Nevermind and Smashing Pumpkins' first albums, shaping the polished, powerful sound of 90s alternative rock. He also co-founded Garbage.
know: He co-founded Smart Studios in Madison, Wisconsin, with Steve Marker.
He is the drummer and a co-founder of the band Garbage.
He also produced Sonic Youth's Dirty, L7's Bricks Are Heavy and Green Day's 21st Century Breakdown.

influencedBy.why: His focus on layered, melodic pop production follows the Beatles' studio craft.
His polished, layered studio approach follows George Martin's model of producer as arranger.
Cheap Trick's heavy Midwest power pop is part of the sound he brought to grunge.

cousins.why: Same polished, heavy, radio-ready production that defined a decade.
Both made loud guitar music sound huge and radio-ready.

artists.name: John Denver
artists.summary: John Denver was a folk-pop singer and songwriter whose warm voice and outdoor themes made him one of the best-selling acts of the 1970s.
know: He wrote "Leaving on a Jet Plane," which Peter, Paul and Mary took to number one in 1969.
Before going solo he sang with the Chad Mitchell Trio.
He won the CMA Entertainer of the Year award in 1975.

influencedBy.why: The Kingston Trio's clean, harmony-based folk pop was the model for the folk groups he started in.
Peter, Paul and Mary shared his producer Milt Okun and turned his song into a hit, launching his career.
Seeger's singalong folk and nature songs set the template for Denver's earnest, audience-friendly style.
Dylan's success made room for folk singers to write their own material, which Denver did from the start.
Denver's warm, nature-minded folk pop follows the style Lightfoot brought to the charts.

cousins.why: Another clean-voiced 1970s crossover star who moved easily between country and pop radio.
Gentle, story-driven crossover songs that topped both country and pop charts.

artists.name: Charley Crockett
artists.summary: Charley Crockett is a Texas singer who blends honky-tonk, blues and soul into a deliberately old-fashioned sound and releases records at a fast clip.
know: He spent years busking in places like the New Orleans French Quarter and the New York subway before recording.
He released a full tribute album to the Texas honky-tonk singer James Hand.
He runs his own label, Son of Davy, and often puts out more than one album a year.
keyAlbums: 10 for Slim: Charley Crockett Sings James Hand

influencedBy.why: Haggard's working-man honky-tonk is the clearest model for Crockett's songwriting and vocal phrasing.
Western swing rhythms and Texas dance-hall feel run through many of his records.
He works in the plain, lonesome honky-tonk tradition that Hank Williams defined.
His blues-leaning sides draw on the Texas country-blues style of Lightnin' Hopkins.
Willie's Texas independence and conversational phrasing are an audible touchstone.
Outlaw-era Waylon is a reference point for his lean, guitar-driven arrangements.

cousins.why: A fellow Texan who revives vintage soul with the same respect for old recording sounds.
Rough-edged Texas songs built for small rooms and road stories.

artists.name: Bo Burnham
artists.summary: Bo Burnham is a comedian and songwriter who went from teenage YouTube videos to the self-made special Inside, mixing jokes with sharp pop songwriting.
know: He started posting comic songs to YouTube in 2006 while still in high school.
He wrote and directed the film Eighth Grade in 2018.
His song "All Eyes on Me" from Inside won a Grammy.

influencedBy.why: Burnham has cited Lehrer as a model for clever, piano-based comedy songs.
Weird Al showed that comedy songs could be built with real pop craft.
Newman's ironic, character-driven piano songs are close kin to Burnham's sharper material.
The Conchords' genre-hopping musical comedy was a contemporary model for Burnham's style parodies.

cousins.why: Another comedian who built a serious music career out of internet-era comedy.
Comedy songs with careful, genre-accurate production.

artists.name: Uncle Dave Macon
artists.summary: Uncle Dave Macon was a banjo-playing showman and the first big star of the Grand Ole Opry, preserving a huge store of 19th-century songs on record.
know: He joined the Grand Ole Opry in 1926 and became its first featured star.
He ran a mule-drawn freight business before turning to music full time.
He was elected to the Country Music Hall of Fame in 1966.
songs: Keep My Skillet Good and Greasy
Way Down the Old Plank Road

cousins.why: A comic, larger-than-life entertainer who was also a serious musician.
A songster from the same early recording era who kept older songs alive.

artists.name: Gene Autry
artists.summary: Gene Autry was the original singing cowboy, a record and film star who made western songs a national craze and recorded some of the best-selling Christmas songs ever.
know: He began as a Jimmie Rodgers-style singer billed as Oklahoma's Yodeling Cowboy on Tulsa radio.
His 1949 recording of "Rudolph the Red-Nosed Reindeer" became one of the top-selling singles of its time.
He later owned the California Angels baseball team.

influencedBy.why: Autry started out closely imitating Rodgers's blue yodels before finding his cowboy style.

cousins.why: A fellow 1930s and 1940s crooner whose Christmas records became perennials.
Easygoing film-and-record star with a relaxed, friendly vocal style.

artists.name: Roy Acuff
artists.summary: Roy Acuff was the Grand Ole Opry's biggest star of the late 1930s and 1940s and, as a publisher, helped build Nashville into the country music business center.
know: He joined the Grand Ole Opry in 1938 and was long called the King of Country Music.
In 1942 he co-founded Acuff-Rose Publishing with songwriter Fred Rose, which later signed Hank Williams.
In 1962 he became the first living person elected to the Country Music Hall of Fame.

influencedBy.why: Acuff came up on the Opry in Macon's shadow and carried on his old-time showmanship.
Acuff's mountain gospel and sacred songs come from the same tradition the Carters put on record.

cousins.why: Gospel-rooted singing that crossed into popular music without losing its church feel.
Train songs and plain-voiced Depression-era singing for working people.

artists.name: Ernest Tubb
artists.summary: Ernest Tubb was a Texas singer who helped define honky-tonk music in the 1940s, put electric guitar at the center of country records, and championed younger artists.
know: Jimmie Rodgers's widow helped launch his career and gave him one of Rodgers's guitars.
His 1941 hit "Walking the Floor Over You" was an early electric-guitar country smash.
He opened the Ernest Tubb Record Shop in Nashville in 1947 and hosted the Midnite Jamboree radio show from it.

influencedBy.why: Tubb began as a devoted Rodgers imitator, and Rodgers's widow personally helped him get started.
Texas dance-hall music shaped the steady, danceable beat of his honky-tonk records.

cousins.why: Simple, steady, instantly recognizable barroom records with plain singing.
Turned up the electric guitar in a rural style and made it the sound of the clubs.

artists.name: The Louvin Brothers
artists.summary: Ira and Charlie Louvin were a brother duo whose high, tight harmonies on gospel and heartbreak songs became a model for country and rock harmony singers.
know: Ira sang the high harmony and played mandolin, while Charlie sang lead and played guitar.
They joined the Grand Ole Opry in 1955.
Their 1959 gospel album Satan Is Real is famous for its homemade cover art.
songs: I Don't Believe You've Met My Baby

influencedBy.why: The Louvins grew up on Acuff's Opry broadcasts and his mix of secular and sacred songs.
The Delmores set the pattern for the brother-duet harmony style the Louvins refined.
Monroe's high lonesome tenor and mandolin shaped Ira's singing and playing.
Much of their gospel and ballad repertoire comes from the Carter Family tradition.

cousins.why: Two-voice harmony as the heart of the sound.
Family harmony singing rooted in gospel.

artists.name: Flatt & Scruggs
artists.summary: Lester Flatt and Earl Scruggs left Bill Monroe's band to form the Foggy Mountain Boys, and Scruggs's three-finger banjo made them bluegrass's most popular act.
know: Both played in Bill Monroe's Blue Grass Boys from about 1945 to 1948.
"The Ballad of Jed Clampett," the Beverly Hillbillies theme, was a number one country hit for them.
"Foggy Mountain Breakdown" was used in the 1967 film Bonnie and Clyde.
songs: Roll in My Sweet Baby's Arms

influencedBy.why: Both men were members of Monroe's band, where the classic bluegrass sound took shape.
They recorded Carter songs, and Maybelle Carter toured with them in the 1960s.

cousins.why: A virtuoso who invented a new way to play his instrument and made it lead.
Tight, instrument-led records that showcase a band's drive.

artists.name: Ralph Stanley
artists.summary: Ralph Stanley co-led the Stanley Brothers and then the Clinch Mountain Boys, keeping a stark mountain style of bluegrass and singing alive for seven decades.
know: From 1967 he led the Clinch Mountain Boys on his own after years co-leading with his brother Carter.
His band was the starting point for Ricky Skaggs and Keith Whitley.
His unaccompanied "O Death" on the O Brother, Where Art Thou? soundtrack won him a Grammy in 2002.

influencedBy.why: His lifelong partnership with his brother Carter formed his whole style.
Monroe's new bluegrass sound shaped the early Stanley Brothers records.
Mountain ballads and gospel from the Carter tradition run through his repertoire.
Produced Stanley's O Death for O Brother.

cousins.why: Raw, spiritual singing with almost no polish.
Sacred music sung with enormous intensity.

artists.name: Doc Watson
artists.summary: Doc Watson was a North Carolina guitarist and singer whose fast, clean flatpicking of fiddle tunes changed how the acoustic guitar is played in folk and bluegrass.
know: He was brought to folk revival audiences in the early 1960s after folklorist Ralph Rinzler recorded him.
He toured and recorded for years with his son Merle, and MerleFest is named for Merle.
He named his son after guitarist Merle Travis.
keyAlbums: Will the Circle Be Unbroken (with Nitty Gritty Dirt Band)

influencedBy.why: Watson learned from Delmore Brothers records, and "Deep River Blues" became a signature tune.
Watson admired Travis enough to name his son after him and absorbed his fingerpicking.
Rodgers's records were among the first country music Watson heard and sang.
Many of his ballads and gospel songs come from the Carter Family repertoire.

cousins.why: Overcame physical limits to become the defining guitarist of his style.
Gentle, rolling guitar and an unhurried voice on old songs.

artists.name: Kitty Wells
artists.summary: Kitty Wells was the first woman to top the country charts as a solo artist and opened the door for women singers in the male-dominated honky-tonk era.
know: "It Wasn't God Who Made Honky Tonk Angels" reached number one in 1952 as an answer song to Hank Thompson's "The Wild Side of Life."
She was billed as the Queen of Country Music.
She was married to Johnnie Wright of the duo Johnnie & Jack.
songs: It Wasn't God Who Made Honky Tonk Angels

influencedBy.why: Her plain, unornamented vocal style comes from the Carter Family's mountain singing.
She came up on the Opry sound Acuff defined.

cousins.why: A woman who broke through in a field run by men and set a new standard.
A woman singer whose plain, direct delivery set the standard for heartbreak songs.

artists.name: Hank Snow
artists.summary: Hank Snow was a Canadian singer and guitarist known as the Singing Ranger, whose fast-talking train songs made him one of country's biggest stars of the 1950s.
know: "I'm Movin' On" spent 21 weeks at number one on the country chart in 1950.
He named his son Jimmie Rodgers Snow after his hero.
His booking agency, run with Colonel Tom Parker, handled an early Elvis Presley tour.

influencedBy.why: Tubb helped bring Snow to the Grand Ole Opry in 1950.
Snow modeled himself on Rodgers and named his son after him.

cousins.why: Fast, rhythmic train and travel songs.
A Canadian storyteller with railroad songs at the core of his catalog.

artists.name: Marty Robbins
artists.summary: Marty Robbins was a versatile country singer best known for his cinematic gunfighter ballads, which brought western story songs back to the top of the charts.
know: "El Paso" won the first Grammy for best country and western recording.
The fuzz-tone guitar on "Don't Worry" came from a faulty amplifier during the session.
He also raced stock cars in NASCAR.
keyAlbums: More Gunfighter Ballads and Trail Songs

influencedBy.why: Robbins grew up on Autry's westerns, and they shaped his cowboy songs.
Rodgers's western and blue-yodel songs were part of his early repertoire.

cousins.why: Big, dramatic ballads sung with a soaring tenor.
A smooth crooner who could sell a story song.

artists.name: Jim Reeves
artists.summary: Jim Reeves was a velvet-voiced singer whose soft, close-miked ballads helped define the polished Nashville sound and made him a star around the world.
know: He worked as an announcer at KWKH, home of the Louisiana Hayride, before his singing career took off.
His RCA records were produced by Chet Atkins.
He was hugely popular abroad, including in the UK, Ireland, Norway and South Africa.

influencedBy.why: Reeves's relaxed, intimate crooning follows Crosby's microphone-based style.
Atkins produced his RCA hits and shaped their smooth arrangements.
Played on He'll Have to Go.

cousins.why: A warm, intimate baritone that crossed every audience.
Easy, velvety ballads for a wide pop audience.

artists.name: Chet Atkins
artists.summary: Chet Atkins was a fingerstyle guitar master and the RCA executive and producer who, with Owen Bradley, built the smooth Nashville sound of the late 1950s and 1960s.
know: He ran RCA Victor's Nashville operation and signed artists including Charley Pride.
He played guitar on early RCA sessions for Elvis Presley.
Gretsch and later Gibson made signature Chet Atkins guitar models.

influencedBy.why: Atkins built his thumb-and-finger picking on Travis's style.
He admired Django's jazz guitar and borrowed from it.
Atkins admired Paul and the two made the album Chester & Lester together.
He played in Mother Maybelle and the Carter Sisters' band around 1950, which brought him to Nashville.

cousins.why: A producer who shaped a whole era's sound from inside a record company.
A musician-producer whose taste set a polished standard for a genre.

artists.name: Owen Bradley
artists.summary: Owen Bradley was the Decca Records producer who, with Chet Atkins, created the Nashville sound, making landmark records with Patsy Cline, Loretta Lynn and Brenda Lee.
know: With his brother Harold he opened a studio on Nashville's 16th Avenue in the 1950s, the start of Music Row.
He headed Decca's Nashville division for years.
He came out of retirement to produce k.d. lang's Shadowland in 1988.

cousins.why: A record-company producer who defined the sound of the stars he recorded.
A producer known for a big, layered signature sound.

artists.name: Billy Sherrill
artists.summary: Billy Sherrill was the Epic Records producer and songwriter behind the lush countrypolitan sound, making classic records with Tammy Wynette, George Jones and Charlie Rich.
know: He co-wrote "Stand by Your Man" with Tammy Wynette.
He produced George Jones's "He Stopped Loving Her Today."
He produced Elvis Costello's country album Almost Blue in 1981.
keyAlbums: I Am What I Am (George Jones)

influencedBy.why: Sherrill's lush countrypolitan productions extended the approach Bradley pioneered.
His big, layered productions are often compared to Spector's wall of sound.

cousins.why: A producer whose signature arrangements defined a label's sound.
Polished, big-budget productions that made stars of singers.

artists.name: Tammy Wynette
artists.summary: Tammy Wynette was a country singer known as the First Lady of Country Music, whose aching voice on Billy Sherrill's lush productions made her one of the genre's defining stars.
know: She worked as a hairdresser before her music career took off.
"Stand by Your Man" became one of the best-selling singles by a woman in country history.
She recorded "Justified and Ancient" with the British group The KLF in 1991.
keyAlbums: Your Good Girl's Gonna Go Bad
songs: 'Til I Can Make It on My Own

influencedBy.why: Wells proved a woman could carry honky-tonk heartbreak songs to the top of the chart.
He signed her, produced her hits and co-wrote her signature song.
Her husband and duet partner, Jones shaped her phrasing on their many records together.
Cline's emotional ballad singing in lush settings paved the way for her sound.

cousins.why: Big, emotional ballad singing that defined a genre's female voice.
Heartbreak songs sung over lush string arrangements.

artists.name: Charley Pride
artists.summary: Charley Pride was a Mississippi-born baritone who became one of RCA's best-selling artists and country music's first Black superstar.
know: He played Negro league baseball, including for the Memphis Red Sox, before singing professionally.
Chet Atkins signed him to RCA in 1965.
In 2000 he became the first Black artist elected to the Country Music Hall of Fame.
songs: Is Anybody Goin' to San Antone
All I Have to Offer You (Is Me)

influencedBy.why: He signed Pride to RCA in 1965.
Pride grew up on Hank's records and kept his songs in his repertoire.
He heard Tubb and other Opry stars on the radio growing up.

cousins.why: Brought a soul singer's warmth to country songs.
A smooth baritone who broke barriers in a mainstream format.

artists.name: Glen Campbell
artists.summary: Glen Campbell was an in-demand Los Angeles session guitarist who became a crossover star singing Jimmy Webb songs like "Wichita Lineman" and "Galveston."
know: As part of the Wrecking Crew he played guitar on records by the Beach Boys, Frank Sinatra and many others.
He filled in for Brian Wilson on Beach Boys tours in the mid-1960s.
He hosted The Glen Campbell Goodtime Hour on TV from 1969 to 1972.
keyAlbums: By the Time I Get to Phoenix
songs: By the Time I Get to Phoenix

influencedBy.why: Campbell often named Django as his favorite guitarist.
His years in the Wrecking Crew taught him studio craft and pop arranging.
Campbell's hit with Gentle on My Mind became one of his signature songs.

cousins.why: Lush, orchestral pop ballads sung with a clear, emotional voice.
Sophisticated pop songcraft with strings and unusual chord changes.

artists.name: Roger Miller
artists.summary: Roger Miller was a witty singer-songwriter whose playful mid-1960s hits like "King of the Road" made him a pop star and a Grammy record-setter.
know: He won 11 Grammys across 1965 and 1966.
He wrote the songs for the Broadway musical Big River, which won the Tony for best score in 1985.
He voiced the rooster narrator in Disney's 1973 Robin Hood.

influencedBy.why: Miller grew up on Hank and started as a Nashville writer in the plain honky-tonk tradition.
He grew up in Oklahoma on western swing and kept its loose, playful rhythm.

cousins.why: Clever wordplay and comic timing in short, catchy songs.
A jokey, swinging entertainer who was also a sharp musician.

artists.name: Bobbie Gentry
artists.summary: Bobbie Gentry was a Mississippi-born singer-songwriter whose mysterious story song "Ode to Billie Joe" made her a star and who wrote and produced much of her own work.
know: She won three Grammys in 1968, including best new artist.
She produced much of her own material, which was rare for a woman at the time.
She recorded a hit duet album with Glen Campbell in 1968.

cousins.why: Southern-tinged soul-pop sung with cool restraint.
Cinematic, atmospheric storytelling with a mysterious persona.

artists.name: Kris Kristofferson
artists.summary: Kris Kristofferson was a Rhodes Scholar turned Nashville songwriter whose literate songs changed what country lyrics could be and who became a film star.
know: He studied at Oxford as a Rhodes Scholar before moving to Nashville.
He worked as a janitor at Columbia's Nashville studios while trying to sell his songs.
He was a member of the Highwaymen with Johnny Cash, Willie Nelson and Waylon Jennings.
keyAlbums: The Silver Tongued Devil and I
songs: Help Me Make It Through the Night

influencedBy.why: Kristofferson often named Hank as the songwriter who drew him to country.
Cash championed him, recorded his songs and later shared the stage in the Highwaymen.
He cited Dylan as the model for writing poetic lyrics within popular song.

cousins.why: A poet who became a songwriter, with a deep, worn voice.
Working-class characters drawn with literary detail.

artists.name: David Allan Coe
artists.summary: David Allan Coe is an outlaw country singer and songwriter known for his rowdy honky-tonk records and for writing hits for other artists.
know: He wrote "Would You Lay with Me (In a Field of Stone)," a number one hit for Tanya Tucker.
He wrote "Take This Job and Shove It," a hit for Johnny Paycheck.
Early in his career he was billed as the Mysterious Rhinestone Cowboy.
songs: You Never Even Called Me by My Name
Would You Lay with Me (In a Field of Stone)

influencedBy.why: Coe's honky-tonk style and song themes return to Hank Williams again and again.
He came up alongside the outlaw movement Waylon led.
Willie's outlaw independence is a direct model, named in his own songs.

cousins.why: Southern rock with a rough honky-tonk attitude.
Bearded Texas-style showmen with a raw roots sound.

artists.name: Jerry Jeff Walker
artists.summary: Jerry Jeff Walker was a New York-born folk singer who wrote "Mr. Bojangles" and became a central figure in the loose, good-time Austin progressive country scene of the 1970s.
know: He wrote "Mr. Bojangles," which the Nitty Gritty Dirt Band made a hit in 1970.
¡Viva Terlingua! was recorded live in the old dance hall in Luckenbach, Texas, in 1973.
His backing group was called the Lost Gonzo Band.
songs: Up Against the Wall, Redneck Mother

influencedBy.why: Walker started as a wandering folk singer in the Guthrie mold.
Dylan's Greenwich Village folk scene was the world Walker came out of.
His close friend Clark supplied several of his best-known songs.

cousins.why: Loose, warm roots music played by a road-tested band.
Easygoing live shows built on community and long jams.

artists.name: Guy Clark
artists.summary: Guy Clark was a Texas songwriter whose carefully crafted, detail-rich songs made him a mentor to generations of country and Americana writers.
know: He built guitars by hand and worked as a luthier.
He was a mentor to younger writers including Steve Earle and Rodney Crowell.
My Favorite Picture of You won the Grammy for best folk album.

influencedBy.why: Van Zandt was his close friend and the songwriter he most measured himself against.
Clark saw Hopkins in Houston clubs and cited him as a formative influence.
His plain-spoken narrative songs come out of the folk tradition Guthrie shaped.

cousins.why: Plain-spoken working-life songs told with exact detail.
A Texas songwriter's songwriter with a long, independent career.

artists.name: Billy Joe Shaver
artists.summary: Billy Joe Shaver was a Texas songwriter whose songs formed the backbone of Waylon Jennings's Honky Tonk Heroes and helped define outlaw country.
know: He wrote nearly all the songs on Waylon Jennings's 1973 album Honky Tonk Heroes.
His debut album was produced by Kris Kristofferson.
In the 1990s he recorded and toured with his son Eddy, a guitarist, in the band Shaver.
keyAlbums: Old Five and Dimers Like Me
songs: Old Five and Dimers Like Me

influencedBy.why: He produced Shaver's debut album.
His plain honky-tonk writing and singing grow straight out of Hank Williams.

cousins.why: Texas songs about hard living, told in a conversational voice.
Rough-voiced storyteller with an eye for down-and-out characters.

artists.name: The Flying Burrito Brothers
artists.summary: The Flying Burrito Brothers, formed by ex-Byrds Gram Parsons and Chris Hillman, fused hard country with rock and soul and laid the foundation for country rock and alt-country.
know: Gram Parsons and Chris Hillman started the band after leaving the Byrds.
Sneaky Pete Kleinow's distorted pedal steel was central to their sound.
They released a version of "Wild Horses" before the Rolling Stones' own came out.
keyAlbums: Last of the Red Hot Burritos

influencedBy.why: Parsons co-founded the band and wrote much of its material.
Founders Parsons and Hillman came straight from the Byrds' Sweetheart of the Rodeo lineup.
Bakersfield country's twang and drive shaped their sound.

Parsons loved the Louvins' close harmonies and gospel songs.
Their two-part harmonies drew on the Everly style.
Their twangy rock was part of the same early country rock push.

cousins.why: Rock musicians reworking American roots styles.
Rock built on country and swamp roots.

artists.name: Nitty Gritty Dirt Band
artists.summary: The Nitty Gritty Dirt Band began as a California jug band and became a bridge between generations with Will the Circle Be Unbroken, which joined them with country's founding figures.
know: They started as a jug band in Southern California in the mid-1960s.

In 1977 they toured the Soviet Union, one of the first American bands to do so.
keyAlbums: Will the Circle Be Unbroken: Volume Two

influencedBy.why: Acuff sang on their 1972 Will the Circle Be Unbroken sessions, linking his generation to theirs.
Earl Scruggs played on their Will the Circle Be Unbroken sessions.
Watson was a central guest on their Will the Circle Be Unbroken sessions.
Their hit version of "Mr. Bojangles" came from his song.
Maybelle Carter played on Will the Circle Be Unbroken, and the title song is a Carter staple.
Travis played and told stories on the Circle sessions.

cousins.why: A rock band reconnecting with older American music.
Roots-minded rock with folk and country underneath.

artists.name: Linda Ronstadt
artists.summary: Linda Ronstadt was one of the best-selling singers of the 1970s, a powerful interpreter who moved from Los Angeles country rock to pop, standards and Mexican music.
know: She first recorded with the folk-rock group the Stone Poneys, who had a hit with "Different Drum."

Canciones de Mi Padre, her 1987 album of Mexican songs, became one of the best-selling non-English albums in the US.
keyAlbums: Trio (with Dolly Parton and Emmylou Harris)

influencedBy.why: She had a major hit with the Everlys' "When Will I Be Loved."
Her close friend and harmony partner, with whom she recorded Trio.
Her hit "Blue Bayou" came from Orbison's songbook.
She recorded his songs and drew on classic country ballad singing.
She recorded Lowell George's Willin', helping make it a country-rock standard.

cousins.why: Polished 1970s California pop-rock built on strong female voices.
A defining Los Angeles canyon-era singer.

artists.name: Kenny Rogers
artists.summary: Kenny Rogers was a Houston-born singer who moved from the rock group the First Edition to become one of the biggest country-pop crossover stars of the late 1970s and 1980s.

The Bee Gees wrote and produced Eyes That See in the Dark.
Rogers often cited Ray Charles's blend of soul and country.

cousins.why: Smooth, ballad-heavy crossover hits of the early 1980s.
A relaxed, friendly voice that crossed every audience.

artists.name: Alabama
artists.summary: Alabama was a band of cousins from Fort Payne who brought a self-contained rock-band model to mainstream country and became one of its best-selling groups.

Their Southern rock band sound has roots in the Allmans' twin-guitar style.

Southern bands with a hometown identity and long careers.

artists.name: Hank Williams Jr.
artists.summary: Hank Williams Jr. started by singing his father's songs and broke away in the mid-1970s to fuse country with Southern rock, becoming a major star of the 1980s.
know: He started performing his father's songs as a child.
Hank Williams Jr. and Friends (1975), with Southern rock musicians, marked his break toward his own style.

Jennings was a friend and model for his move toward outlaw country.
Southern rock bands like the Allmans shaped his mid-1970s reinvention.

cousins.why: Loud, guitar-driven Southern pride songs.

artists.name: Ricky Skaggs

She helped bring Joni Mitchell back to the stage, hosting the Joni Jam sessions and Mitchell's 2022 Newport Folk Festival set.
keyAlbums: By the Way, I Forgive You

influencedBy.why: Carlile's roots rock and emotional directness follow Williams's lead.
Carlile has called Elton John her biggest musical hero and later made an album with him.
Carlile has performed Mitchell's Blue in full and became a close collaborator and champion of hers.
She has said Patsy Cline was one of the first voices she tried to copy as a child.
Burnett produced The Story and captured her band live in the studio.
Cobb co-produced By the Way, I Forgive You with Shooter Jennings, giving it a warm, orchestral roots sound.
Carlile has cited Freddie Mercury and Queen as an influence on her dramatic vocal style.

cousins.why: Both are known for huge, emotional voices on piano and guitar ballads.
Both have big, clear voices that move easily between country, folk and pop.

artists.name: Margo Price
artists.summary: Margo Price is an Illinois-born singer and songwriter who broke through in Nashville with a classic honky-tonk sound and frank, personal songs. She became one of the leading voices of 2010s independent country.
know: Her debut Midwest Farmer's Daughter was released on Jack White's Third Man Records.
Sturgill Simpson produced her third album, That's How Rumors Get Started.
She was nominated for the Grammy for Best New Artist and later published a memoir, Maybe We'll Make It.

influencedBy.why: Price's raw, honest country songwriting draws on the Americana path Williams opened.
Price has named Lynn as a hero, and her frank songs about working-class life follow Lynn's model.
Her honky-tonk shuffles and blue-collar themes draw directly on Haggard's Bakersfield country.
Nelson sang a duet with her on Learning to Lose and has been a mentor and touring partner.
Simpson produced That's How Rumors Get Started and pushed her toward a bigger rock sound.
Kristofferson's plain, poetic songwriting is a model for her more reflective songs.
Harris' blend of traditional country and rock harmonies runs through Price's records.

cousins.why: Both write fierce, personal songs with a rebellious streak.
Both came through Jack White's world with a raw, retro sound.

artists.name: The Kingston Trio
artists.summary: The Kingston Trio was a clean-cut California group whose 1958 hit Tom Dooley set off the folk boom of the late 1950s and early 1960s. Their tight harmonies and acoustic guitars and banjo brought folk songs to the pop charts.
know: Tom Dooley, an old North Carolina ballad, went to No. 1 and won them a Grammy.
At one point in 1959 they had four albums in the Billboard top ten at once.
The original lineup was Dave Guard, Bob Shane and Nick Reynolds, with John Stewart replacing Guard in 1961.
songs: Where Have All the Flowers Gone

influencedBy.why: The Weavers had already shown that folk songs with group harmonies could reach the pop charts.
Belafonte's calypso hits inspired the group's name and their early calypso numbers.
They recorded Seeger's Where Have All the Flowers Gone and drew on his banjo-led folk repertoire.
Guthrie's songs were part of the American folk songbook they adapted for pop audiences.
Lead Belly's songs, many collected and passed on through the folk scene, were part of the material they drew from.

cousins.why: Both made clean, close-harmony records that topped the late 1950s charts.
Both were polished harmony groups who turned traditional tunes into pop hits.

artists.name: Peter, Paul and Mary
artists.summary: Peter, Paul and Mary was a Greenwich Village trio of Peter Yarrow, Noel Paul Stookey and Mary Travers. Their harmonies carried protest and folk songs, including early Bob Dylan, to a mass audience.
know: The trio was put together by manager Albert Grossman, who also managed Bob Dylan.
Their version of Blowin' in the Wind became a top-ten hit in 1963.
Their only No. 1 single was Leaving on a Jet Plane, a song written by John Denver.

influencedBy.why: Peter, Paul and Mary followed the trio's model of a polished folk harmony act on the pop charts.
If I Had a Hammer was written by Weavers members Pete Seeger and Lee Hays, and the trio's group harmony follows the Weavers.
They took many songs and the idea of folk music as social action from Seeger.
They shared a manager with Dylan and helped launch him by recording his songs.
Guthrie's songs and spirit were part of the folk songbook they drew on.
They recorded Freight Train, spreading it to a large audience.

cousins.why: Both blend male and female voices into bright, carefully arranged harmonies.
Both sang songs tied to the civil rights movement to big audiences.

artists.name: The Weavers
artists.summary: The Weavers were a New York folk quartet of Pete Seeger, Lee Hays, Ronnie Gilbert and Fred Hellerman. Their early 1950s hits brought traditional and world folk songs to pop radio and laid the ground for the folk revival.
know: Their version of Lead Belly's Goodnight, Irene topped the charts for months in 1950.
They were blacklisted during the early 1950s Red Scare, which cut off much of their radio and TV work.
A 1955 reunion concert at Carnegie Hall, released as a live album, revived their career.

influencedBy.why: Seeger knew Lead Belly, and the group's biggest hit was his Goodnight, Irene.
Seeger and Hays sang with Guthrie in the Almanac Singers, the group that led to the Weavers.
Seeger was a founding member and the group's banjo player and main song collector.
The Carter Family's old-time songs were part of the American folk repertoire the group drew from.

cousins.why: Both were vocal groups who brought folk and spiritual songs to big audiences with tight harmonies.
Both turned traditional folk songs into singalongs for large crowds.

artists.name: Ramblin' Jack Elliott
artists.summary: Ramblin' Jack Elliott is a Brooklyn-born folk singer who learned directly from Woody Guthrie and carried his songs and style to a new generation. He was a key bridge between Guthrie and the folk revival, both in America and Britain.
know: As a teenager he ran away to join a rodeo, which started his lifelong love of cowboy songs.
He lived and traveled with Woody Guthrie in the early 1950s and learned his repertoire firsthand.
He spent several years playing in Britain in the late 1950s, where young skiffle and folk players heard him.
keyAlbums: Jack Elliott Sings the Songs of Woody Guthrie
songs: Don't Think Twice, It's All Right

influencedBy.why: Elliott lived with Guthrie, learned his songs and guitar style, and became his best-known disciple.
Rodgers' blue yodels and train songs, such as Muleskinner Blues, are a big part of Elliott's repertoire.
Lead Belly's twelve-string songs were part of the New York folk scene where Elliott learned to play.
The singing-cowboy records Elliott loved as a boy shaped his lifelong focus on cowboy songs.

cousins.why: Both are rambling storytellers who kept old American work and train songs alive.
Both sing cowboy songs with an easy, conversational style.

artists.name: Dave Van Ronk
artists.summary: Dave Van Ronk was a Brooklyn-born singer and guitarist who was a central figure of the Greenwich Village folk scene. His fingerpicked blues and big, gravelly voice made him a teacher and mentor to many younger folk musicians.
know: He was nicknamed the Mayor of MacDougal Street, which became the title of his memoir.
Bob Dylan learned Van Ronk's arrangement of House of the Rising Sun and recorded it on his first album.
The 2013 film Inside Llewyn Davis was loosely inspired by his memoir and the Village scene.
keyAlbums: Dave Van Ronk Sings Ballads, Blues and a Spiritual
songs: He Was a Friend of Mine

influencedBy.why: Lead Belly's songs and twelve-string style were part of Van Ronk's early folk education.
Van Ronk's fingerpicked country blues owes a lot to John Hurt's gentle, rolling guitar.
Van Ronk started in traditional jazz and drew his big blues vocal style from classic singers like Bessie Smith.
His early work in New Orleans-style jazz bands drew on Morton's songs and style.
McTell's ragtime-flavored blues guitar was part of the repertoire Van Ronk mastered.
Van Ronk described the Anthology as a central text for the Greenwich Village folk scene.
Van Ronk cited White's guitar playing and arrangements as a model.

cousins.why: Both are master fingerpicking guitarists who mixed ragtime and blues.
Both used big, gravelly voices to bring early American blues and jazz songs to life.

artists.name: Phil Ochs
artists.summary: Phil Ochs was a Texas-born singer and songwriter who became one of the leading topical songwriters of the 1960s Greenwich Village scene. He wrote pointed songs about the news of the day and later moved toward more orchestral, personal records.
know: He studied journalism at Ohio State University and called himself a singing journalist.
Joan Baez had a hit with his song There but for Fortune.
His 1967 album Pleasures of the Harbor added lush orchestral arrangements to his songs.
keyAlbums: All the News That's Fit to Sing

influencedBy.why: Guthrie's songs about current events were the model for Ochs' topical writing.
Seeger's idea of folk music as social action shaped Ochs' whole approach.
Ochs was a friend and rival of Dylan in the Village, and Dylan's early topical songs pushed him forward.
Ochs was a lifelong Elvis fan and even performed in a gold suit as a tribute.
Ochs admired Cash's plain storytelling and his country songs about ordinary people.

cousins.why: Both wrote sharp, news-driven songs about politics and society.
Both put current events and protest at the center of their songs.

artists.name: Judy Collins
artists.summary: Judy Collins is a singer known for her clear soprano and her ear for great songs by other writers. In the 1960s she helped launch the careers of Leonard Cohen and Joni Mitchell by recording their songs.
know: She trained as a classical pianist as a girl under conductor Antonia Brico.
Her recording of Joni Mitchell's Both Sides Now became a top-ten hit and won a Grammy.
Stephen Stills wrote Suite: Judy Blue Eyes about her.
keyAlbums: Who Knows Where the Time Goes

influencedBy.why: Collins started in the folk revival, singing traditional and topical songs in the style Seeger spread.
The Weavers' popular folk records were part of what drew her from classical piano to folk.
Collins has said hearing Guthrie's songs helped turn her toward folk music.
Her early albums, especially Judy Collins #3, leaned heavily on Dylan's songs.
Baez's clear soprano and interpretive approach were the main model for female folk singers of Collins' generation.

cousins.why: Both are great interpreters who made other writers' songs into hits.
Both are known for pure, expressive voices and careful song choices.

artists.name: Gordon Lightfoot
artists.summary: Gordon Lightfoot was a Canadian singer and songwriter from Orillia, Ontario, who came up in Toronto's coffeehouse scene. His story songs and warm baritone made him one of the most respected songwriters of the 1960s and 1970s.
know: Early songs such as Early Morning Rain and For Lovin' Me became hits for other artists, including Peter, Paul and Mary.
The CBC commissioned his Canadian Railroad Trilogy for Canada's centennial in 1967.
His album Sundown and its title track both reached No. 1 in the United States in 1974.
songs: If You Could Read My Mind
The Wreck of the Edmund Fitzgerald

influencedBy.why: Lightfoot said hearing Dylan showed him that folk songs could be personal and pushed him to write his own.
Seeger's folk songs and banjo-and-guitar style were among Lightfoot's early models.
The Weavers' popular folk records shaped Lightfoot's early sense of what a folk song could be.
Fellow Canadian Hank Snow's country storytelling and train songs fit Lightfoot's own travel ballads.

cousins.why: Both had warm voices and wistful, guitar-driven hits about the road and home.
Both made rootsy, story-driven music that grew out of Ontario.

artists.name: Buffy Sainte-Marie
artists.summary: Buffy Sainte-Marie is a singer and songwriter who rose in the Greenwich Village folk scene of the 1960s. Her songs about war, Indigenous rights and love were widely covered, and she was an early adopter of electronic sounds in folk.
know: Her anti-war song Universal Soldier became a hit for Donovan in 1965.
She co-wrote Up Where We Belong, which won the Academy Award for Best Original Song.
Her 1969 album Illuminations used electronic processing on her voice and guitar, unusual for a folk record at the time.
songs: Until It's Time for You to Go

influencedBy.why: Her protest songs come out of the topical folk tradition Seeger led.
Guthrie's songs about injustice set the pattern for the folk revival writers she came up with.
Odetta's powerful voice and serious songs shaped the coffeehouse scene where Sainte-Marie started.

cousins.why: Both used folk music to speak about their people and their rights to a world audience.
Both wrote and sang fiercely political songs alongside tender ballads.

artists.name: Fairport Convention
artists.summary: Fairport Convention is the London band that invented British folk rock by playing traditional English ballads with electric instruments. Their 1969 album Liege & Lief is widely seen as the founding record of the genre.
know: They started out covering American songwriters such as Bob Dylan and Joni Mitchell before turning to English tradition.
Members over the years included Sandy Denny, Richard Thompson, Ashley Hutchings and fiddler Dave Swarbrick.
They have hosted the Cropredy Convention folk festival in Oxfordshire nearly every year since the late 1970s.
keyAlbums: What We Did on Our Holidays
songs: Who Knows Where the Time Goes?

influencedBy.why: The Byrds' electric take on folk songs was the starting model for the young band.
They covered Dylan heavily in their early years, including songs from his unreleased tapes.
They were among the first to record Joni Mitchell songs, before her own albums came out.
Hearing The Band's rootsy Music from Big Pink pushed them to look to their own English traditions.
Denny joined in 1968 and her voice and songs shaped the band's best-known records.

cousins.why: Both turned old folk songs into electric rock.
Both keep traditional British Isles tunes alive for modern audiences.

artists.name: Sandy Denny
artists.summary: Sandy Denny was an English singer and songwriter often called the finest voice of British folk rock. She sang with Fairport Convention, led her own band Fotheringay and wrote Who Knows Where the Time Goes?
know: She is the only guest singer ever to appear on a Led Zeppelin album, on The Battle of Evermore.
She first recorded Who Knows Where the Time Goes? with the Strawbs before Judy Collins made it a hit.
Melody Maker readers voted her the top British female singer in 1970 and 1971.
keyAlbums: The North Star Grassman and the Ravens
songs: Who Knows Where the Time Goes?

influencedBy.why: Her bandmates in Fairport, especially Richard Thompson, shaped her move into electric folk.
Denny started out in London folk clubs singing in the style of American revival singers like Baez.
Dylan's songs were part of her early folk club repertoire and recordings.
Mitchell's personal, piano-and-guitar songwriting is a close parallel to Denny's own writing.
Collins' pure, interpretive soprano was a model for folk singers of Denny's generation.

cousins.why: Both wrote warm, personal songs at the piano and sang them with deep feeling.
Both have haunting, slow, folk-tinged songs carried by a lingering voice.

artists.name: Bert Jansch
artists.summary: Bert Jansch was a Scottish guitarist and singer whose complex fingerpicking changed acoustic guitar playing in Britain and beyond. He was a solo artist and a co-founder of the folk-jazz band Pentangle.
know: He co-founded Pentangle with fellow guitarist John Renbourn in the late 1960s.
Jimmy Page based Led Zeppelin's Black Mountain Side on Jansch's arrangement of the folk song Blackwaterside.
Neil Young has called him one of the greatest acoustic guitar players.

influencedBy.why: Broonzy's blues guitar, heard on records and British tours, shaped Jansch's early playing.
Jansch and Pentangle drew on modern jazz, and they recorded Mingus' Goodbye Pork Pie Hat.
The skiffle boom Donegan sparked got a generation of British teenagers, Jansch included, to pick up guitars.

cousins.why: Both are acoustic guitar masters with a style other players spent years trying to copy.
Both drew on traditional music from Scotland and Ireland and gave it new life.

artists.name: Jackson Browne
artists.summary: Jackson Browne is a Los Angeles singer and songwriter whose introspective songs defined the 1970s Southern California sound. He wrote for and helped shape the Eagles and produced Warren Zevon's early albums.
know: As a teenager he was briefly a member of the Nitty Gritty Dirt Band.
He co-wrote Take It Easy with Glenn Frey, which became the Eagles' first single.
He produced Warren Zevon's 1976 debut and Excitable Boy.

influencedBy.why: Browne has cited Dylan as the songwriter who showed him what a song could say.
He played with the Dirt Band as a teenager, his first real band experience.
The Byrds' folk rock was the Los Angeles sound Browne grew up in.
Cohen's literary, introspective songs are a clear model for Browne's early writing.
Mitchell's confessional songs set the tone for the Laurel Canyon writers Browne came up with.

cousins.why: Both wrote personal, plain-spoken songs that defined 1970s singer-songwriter rock.
Both are California rock songwriters with heartfelt, guitar-driven songs.

artists.name: Jim Croce
artists.summary: Jim Croce was a Philadelphia singer and songwriter known for warm character songs and tender ballads. In a short career in the early 1970s he scored several of the era's best-loved hits.
know: Guitarist Maury Muehleisen played the intricate lead acoustic parts on most of his records.
Bad, Bad Leroy Brown reached No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100 in 1973.
He worked a long list of day jobs, including truck driving and construction, which fed his songs about ordinary people.
keyAlbums: You Don't Mess Around with Jim
songs: You Don't Mess Around with Jim
Operator (That's Not the Way It Feels)

influencedBy.why: Croce's gentle, story-driven folk hits share Lightfoot's approach to the radio ballad.
Croce came up in the folk revival, and Guthrie's songs about working people shaped his character writing.
Dylan's success showed folk singers like Croce that original songs could reach the charts.

cousins.why: Both wrote warm, plain-spoken songs about everyday people with an acoustic heart.
Both are storytellers who built hits around vivid working-class characters.

artists.name: Randy Newman
artists.summary: Randy Newman is a Los Angeles songwriter and composer known for witty, ironic songs sung in character and for his film scores. He moved from cult-favorite albums in the 1970s to scoring many Pixar films, including Toy Story.
know: He comes from a family of Hollywood film composers, including his uncles Alfred, Lionel and Emil Newman.
He wrote You've Got a Friend in Me for Toy Story and has won two Academy Awards for Best Original Song.
He started as a teenage staff songwriter for a publishing company, writing songs for other singers.
songs: You've Got a Friend in Me
I Think It's Going to Rain Today

influencedBy.why: Newman has said Ray Charles was his biggest influence as a singer and pianist.
His rolling New Orleans piano style owes a lot to Fats Domino.
Newman's mix of popular song and orchestral writing follows in the line of Gershwin.
Toussaint's New Orleans arranging and piano feel run through Newman's Southern-themed records.

cousins.why: Both are witty songwriters who use sly wordplay and sharp irony.
Both write ironic, sophisticated songs that play with dark humor.

artists.name: Warren Zevon
artists.summary: Warren Zevon was a Chicago-born singer and songwriter who made his name in the 1970s Los Angeles scene. He was known for darkly funny, literate songs and his hit Werewolves of London.
know: Before his solo breakthrough he worked as bandleader and keyboard player for the Everly Brothers.
Jackson Browne produced his 1976 self-titled album and Excitable Boy.
Linda Ronstadt had hits with several of his songs, including Poor Poor Pitiful Me.

influencedBy.why: Browne championed and produced Zevon's first two major-label albums.
Zevon toured as the Everlys' bandleader, and their harmony pop shaped his melodies.
Dylan's literate, wordy songs were a key model for Zevon's writing.
Newman's ironic, piano-based songs in character are a close ancestor of Zevon's style.

cousins.why: Both write dark, literate story songs with a sharp sense of humor.
Both are clever, sardonic songwriters with rock band muscle.

artists.name: Tom Waits
artists.summary: Tom Waits is a California singer and songwriter known for his gravelly voice and his move from jazzy barroom ballads to junkyard experimental rock. His records from the 1980s onward, made with partner Kathleen Brennan, are some of the most distinctive in American music.
know: The Eagles covered his song Ol' '55 on their album On the Border.
Swordfishtrombones in 1983 began his shift to strange percussion and unusual instruments.
He was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2011.

influencedBy.why: Waits came up in the same Los Angeles scene, and Newman's in-character piano songs are a clear parallel.
Beefheart's raw, clattering blues was a widely noted influence on Waits' 1980s sound.
Waits' growling vocal style draws on Howlin' Wolf's rough blues delivery.
His gravelly voice and love of old jazz recall Louis Armstrong's singing.
Dylan's wordy, character-filled songs were an early model for Waits' writing.
Waits recorded two of his songs for the 2016 tribute album God Don't Never Change.

cousins.why: Both mix gravelly voices with old-time New Orleans and barroom sounds.
Both play louche, offbeat characters in songs that blend jazz and pop.

artists.name: Ani DiFranco
artists.summary: Ani DiFranco is a Buffalo singer, songwriter and guitarist known for her percussive playing and fiercely independent career. She founded her own label as a teenager and became a model for do-it-yourself musicians.
know: She founded Righteous Babe Records in 1990 to release her own music.
Her guitar style uses hard, percussive strumming, often with alternate tunings.
She toured relentlessly through the 1990s and built a large following almost entirely without major-label support.

influencedBy.why: Mitchell's personal songs and open-tuned guitar are a clear model for DiFranco.
DiFranco has named Seeger as a hero and has performed his songs.
Guthrie's political folk songs set the pattern for DiFranco's activist writing.
Dylan's mix of protest and personal songs is a root of her style.

cousins.why: Both ran their own labels and toured on their own terms.
Both are fierce, poetic performers who mix politics and the personal.

artists.name: Conor Oberst
artists.summary: Conor Oberst is an Omaha singer and songwriter best known as the leader of Bright Eyes. His raw, wordy songs made him a central figure of 2000s indie folk and the Saddle Creek Records scene.
know: He began releasing home-recorded tapes as a young teenager in Omaha.
He was part of the circle that built Saddle Creek Records, home to Bright Eyes and other Omaha bands.
He formed Better Oblivion Community Center with Phoebe Bridgers and the supergroup Monsters of Folk with Jim James and M. Ward.
keyAlbums: Lifted or The Story Is in the Soil, Keep Your Ear to the Ground (Bright Eyes)
I'm Wide Awake, It's Morning (Bright Eyes)

influencedBy.why: Oberst's wordy, harmonica-backed folk songs draw heavily on early Dylan.
Harris sang harmony on several songs on I'm Wide Awake, It's Morning.
Smith's quiet, confessional indie folk is a close model for Oberst's softer songs.
Neutral Milk Hotel's raw, emotional folk-punk shaped the late 1990s indie scene Bright Eyes came out of.

cousins.why: Both made emotional, literate indie records in the 2000s.
Both deliver strange, intense lyrics with a cracked, urgent voice.

artists.name: Joanna Newsom
artists.summary: Joanna Newsom is a California harpist, singer and songwriter known for long, dense songs and an unusual voice. Her orchestral album Ys is one of the most acclaimed indie records of the 2000s.
know: She plays the concert pedal harp and studied composition at Mills College.
Van Dyke Parks wrote the orchestral arrangements for Ys, and Steve Albini recorded her harp and vocals.
Her triple album Have One on Me runs more than two hours.

influencedBy.why: Albini recorded the harp and vocals on Ys with a clear, natural sound.
Mitchell's long, poetic songs and unusual harmonies are a clear ancestor of Newsom's writing.
Bush's adventurous, high-voiced art pop is a frequent point of comparison for Newsom's style.
The old American ballads gathered on Smith's Anthology of American Folk Music fed Newsom's interest in early folk song.

cousins.why: Both make ambitious, highly personal music with unusual voices and arrangements.
Both create dreamy, ornate music where the voice is used as an instrument.

artists.name: The Tallest Man on Earth
artists.summary: The Tallest Man on Earth is the stage name of Swedish singer and guitarist Kristian Matsson. His fast fingerpicking and raspy voice made him a favorite of the 2010s indie folk scene.
know: Matsson is from Leksand in the Dalarna region of Sweden.
He built his early following with solo shows of just voice and acoustic guitar or banjo.
He has toured with Bon Iver and other leading indie folk acts.

influencedBy.why: Matsson's raspy voice and fast, wordy acoustic songs are often compared to early Dylan.
Matsson has named Nick Drake as an early influence on his open-tuned guitar playing.
His intricate fingerpicking follows the British folk guitar style Jansch made famous.

cousins.why: Both sing raw, urgent songs over driving acoustic guitar.
Both draw on Dylan-style songwriting with a modern indie feel.

artists.name: Father John Misty
artists.summary: Father John Misty is the stage name of Josh Tillman, a former Fleet Foxes drummer who reinvented himself as a sardonic Los Angeles singer and songwriter. His lush, 1970s-style records mix biting humor with sincere love songs.
know: He was the drummer for Fleet Foxes from 2008 to 2012.
Jonathan Wilson produced and played on his debut as Father John Misty, Fear Fun.
He has co-written songs for Lady Gaga and Beyoncé.
songs: Chateau Lobby #4 (in C for Two Virgins)

influencedBy.why: His sardonic, character-driven songs over orchestral backing follow Randy Newman closely.
Tillman drummed and sang harmony in Fleet Foxes before going solo.
Cohen's wry, literary love songs are a model for Tillman's writing.
His piano-led, 1970s-style ballads echo early Elton John.
Lennon's mix of personal confession and social comment runs through Pure Comedy.

cousins.why: Both make lush, cinematic records full of Los Angeles nostalgia and irony.
Both are literate, theatrical songwriters who blend romance and dark humor.

artists.name: Tom Lehrer
artists.summary: Tom Lehrer was a Harvard-trained mathematician who wrote and sang witty, satirical songs at the piano. A small body of work from the 1950s and 1960s made him one of the most influential musical comedians in America.
know: He taught mathematics at Harvard, MIT and the University of California, Santa Cruz.
He paid to record and release his first album himself in 1953.
In 2020 he placed his songs and lyrics into the public domain.
keyAlbums: An Evening Wasted with Tom Lehrer
That Was the Year That Was

influencedBy.why: Lehrer's tight wordplay and clever rhymes follow the Broadway tradition of Cole Porter.
His piano songs borrow the shape of classic American popular song as written by Berlin.
Lehrer's show-tune melodies come straight out of the Broadway songwriting of Gershwin's era.

cousins.why: Both used sharp satire and real musical skill to poke fun at society.
Both made comic story songs that are as funny as they are musical.

artists.name: Shel Silverstein
artists.summary: Shel Silverstein was a Chicago cartoonist, children's author and songwriter whose funny, offbeat songs became hits for other artists. He wrote A Boy Named Sue for Johnny Cash and many songs for Dr. Hook.
know: He wrote the beloved children's books The Giving Tree and Where the Sidewalk Ends.
Johnny Cash's live recording of A Boy Named Sue became a top-five pop hit and won Silverstein a Grammy for songwriting.
His song I'm Checkin' Out, from the film Postcards from the Edge, was nominated for an Academy Award.
songs: The Cover of the Rolling Stone

influencedBy.why: Lehrer showed that witty, satirical songs could find a wide audience, a path Silverstein followed.
Silverstein came out of the folk revival, where Guthrie's talking songs and humor were central.
His early folk records drew on the singalong folk songbook Seeger spread.

cousins.why: Both wrote clever, funny country-tinged songs full of wordplay.
Both wrote comic story songs that became hits for other performers.

artists.name: "Weird Al" Yankovic
artists.summary: "Weird Al" Yankovic is an accordion-playing singer and songwriter famous for his parodies of pop hits and his original style pastiches. He is the most successful comedy musician of the music video era.
know: He got his start sending home-recorded tapes to the Dr. Demento radio show as a teenager.
Mandatory Fun in 2014 became the first comedy album to debut at No. 1 on the Billboard 200.
He asks permission from the original artists before releasing his parodies.

influencedBy.why: Yankovic has named Lehrer as an early influence on his comic songwriting.
Yankovic grew up on the same kind of comic songs Silverstein wrote and performed.
Yankovic is a Zappa fan, and his Genius in France pastiche honors Zappa's style.
His original song Dare to Be Stupid is a pastiche of Devo's quirky new wave sound.

cousins.why: Both are fun, quirky acts who never take themselves too seriously.
Both mix jokes, pop culture and real musical craft in playful songs.

artists.name: Flight of the Conchords
artists.summary: Flight of the Conchords is the New Zealand comedy duo of Bret McKenzie and Jemaine Clement. Their deadpan acoustic songs that spoof different genres became famous through their HBO series.
know: Their HBO series about the duo trying to make it in New York ran from 2007 to 2009.
Their EP The Distant Future won the Grammy for Best Comedy Album.
Bret McKenzie won an Academy Award for writing Man or Muppet for The Muppets.
keyAlbums: I Told You I Was Freaky

influencedBy.why: The Conchords follow Lehrer's model of deadpan, musically skilled comedy songs.
The Conchords' genre parodies follow the style pastiche approach Yankovic perfected.
Their song Bowie is a loving pastiche of Bowie's sounds and personas.
Their gentle two-voice acoustic folk often nods to Simon & Garfunkel.
Foux du Fafa spoofs breezy French pop in the style of Gainsbourg.

cousins.why: Both hop between genres for laughs while playing each style with real skill.
Both pair witty, offbeat lyrics with clever musical pastiche.

artists.name: Jerry Reed
artists.summary: Jerry Reed was an Atlanta-born guitarist, singer and songwriter known for his dazzling thumb-picking and good-humored hits. He was also a film actor, best known for Smokey and the Bandit.
know: Elvis Presley recorded Reed's Guitar Man and U.S. Male, with Reed playing guitar on Guitar Man.
He sang East Bound and Down for Smokey and the Bandit and played a lead role in the film.
His duet album Me & Jerry with Chet Atkins won a Grammy for Best Country Instrumental Performance.
keyAlbums: The Unbelievable Guitar and Voice of Jerry Reed

influencedBy.why: He produced Reed and recorded duet albums with him.
Reed's thumb-picking style grows straight out of Travis picking.
Les Paul's inventive electric guitar showmanship was part of the guitar world Reed grew up in.

cousins.why: Both were guitar heroes who wrote witty, story-driven songs.
Both built a signature sound around playing with the thumb.

artists.name: John Hartford
artists.summary: John Hartford was a banjo player, fiddler and songwriter who wrote Gentle on My Mind and helped invent progressive bluegrass. His 1971 album Aereo-Plain is a founding record of newgrass.
know: Glen Campbell's version of his Gentle on My Mind became a hit and won Hartford Grammy Awards.
He was a regular on The Smothers Brothers Comedy Hour and The Glen Campbell Goodtime Hour.
A lifelong lover of the Mississippi River, he was a licensed steamboat pilot.
songs: Up on the Hill Where They Do the Boogie

influencedBy.why: Hartford's banjo-and-storytelling act drew directly on the old Opry songster tradition Macon embodied.
Hartford's banjo style grew directly out of the Scruggs approach.
Monroe's bluegrass was the foundation Hartford built on and later stretched.
The Stanleys' old mountain sound was part of the tradition Hartford loved and drew on.
Watson's mix of old-time songs and folk revival appeal fit Hartford's own approach.

cousins.why: Both loved bluegrass and stretched it into loose, exploratory music.
Both played warm, good-time music rooted in jug band and folk styles.

artists.name: Béla Fleck
artists.summary: Béla Fleck is a banjo virtuoso who has taken the instrument into bluegrass, jazz fusion, classical and African music. With his band the Flecktones he showed what the banjo could do far beyond its roots.
know: He was named after the Hungarian composer Béla Bartók.
He played in New Grass Revival before forming Béla Fleck and the Flecktones with bassist Victor Wooten.
He has been nominated for Grammy Awards in more categories than almost any other musician.

influencedBy.why: Fleck has said hearing the Beverly Hillbillies theme made him want to play banjo.
Watson's flatpicking set the bar for the newgrass virtuosity Fleck's generation pursued.
Fleck came up in the newgrass movement that Hartford's Aereo-Plain helped start.
Monroe's bluegrass is the tradition Fleck learned before branching out.
The Flecktones' jazz fusion grooves draw on the fusion bands of the 1970s like Weather Report.

cousins.why: Both are virtuosos who took a plucked string instrument far beyond its home tradition.
Both blend jazz virtuosity with a wide range of other styles.

artists.name: Delia Derbyshire
artists.summary: A composer at the BBC Radiophonic Workshop who built sounds from tape loops and oscillators. Her 1963 realisation of the Doctor Who theme made electronic music part of everyday British life.
know: She turned Ron Grainer's written score for the Doctor Who theme into sound by cutting and splicing tape by hand.
She studied mathematics and music at Cambridge before joining the BBC.
With David Vorhaus and Brian Hodgson she made the 1969 album An Electric Storm as White Noise.

cousins.why: Another British tape pioneer who built otherworldly sounds by hand in the early 1960s.
A studio inventor who treated tape itself as an instrument.

artists.name: Wendy Carlos
artists.summary: A composer and engineer who showed what the Moog synthesizer could do with Switched-On Bach. Her later film scores for Stanley Kubrick and Tron set a template for electronic soundtracks.
know: Switched-On Bach was one of the first classical albums to sell over a million copies and won three Grammys.
She worked closely with Robert Moog, suggesting changes to his early instruments.
She scored A Clockwork Orange, The Shining and Tron.
songs: Title Music from A Clockwork Orange

cousins.why: A one-person studio project that brought classical scale to new technology.
An inventor-musician who changed how records were made.

artists.name: Silver Apples
artists.summary: A New York duo of oscillators and drums whose two late-1960s albums sound years ahead of their time. They are a key link between psychedelia and later electronic rock.
know: Simeon Coxe played a homemade rig of oscillators and switches that the band called The Simeon.
Danny Taylor played hypnotic, repetitive drum patterns under the electronic drones.
They made two albums for Kapp Records before splitting, then Simeon revived the name in the 1990s.

cousins.why: Krautrock built on the same steady, hypnotic pulse.
Another band that fused rock drumming with repetition and experiment.

artists.name: Tangerine Dream
artists.summary: Edgar Froese's Berlin group defined the sequencer-driven Berlin School of electronic music in the 1970s. They later became prolific film composers.
know: Klaus Schulze played drums on their 1970 debut Electronic Meditation.
Phaedra, built on Moog sequencer patterns, reached the UK top 20 in 1974.
They scored films including Sorcerer, Thief and Risky Business.

influencedBy.why: Their early long space-rock pieces drew on Pink Floyd's psychedelic experiments.
Schulze was a founding bandmate on the first album.

cousins.why: German cosmic music with film score ties.
Long instrumental suites that sold to a rock audience.

artists.name: Jean-Michel Jarre
artists.summary: A French composer whose 1976 album Oxygène took instrumental synthesizer music to the top of the charts. He is also known for huge outdoor concerts with lights and lasers.
know: He studied at Pierre Schaeffer's Groupe de Recherches Musicales in Paris.
He is the son of film composer Maurice Jarre.
His 2015 album Electronica 1 paired him with artists such as Air, Moby and Massive Attack's 3D.

influencedBy.why: Her synthesizer albums opened a mass market for the instrumental electronic records Jarre made.
Jarre's sequenced instrumental albums follow the space-music template they set.

cousins.why: Instrumental albums that became mainstream hits.
Big concept records presented with large light shows.

artists.name: Klaus Schulze
artists.summary: A Berlin drummer turned synthesizer composer who made long, slowly unfolding electronic pieces. His 1970s albums are core texts of the Berlin School.
know: He drummed on Tangerine Dream's first album and co-founded Ash Ra Tempel.
His albums often hold just one or two tracks that each fill a full side.
He also recorded under the name Richard Wahnfried.

influencedBy.why: Schulze's solo Berlin School work grew out of his time in the band.
His early long-form pieces grew out of the same space-rock moment as Pink Floyd.

cousins.why: Slow, meditative German music made with early synthesizers.
Fellow German electronic pioneers of the early 1970s.

artists.name: Vangelis
artists.summary: A Greek composer who moved from the rock band Aphrodite's Child to lush synthesizer albums and film scores. His music for Chariots of Fire and Blade Runner is among the best known electronic film music.
know: He was a founding member of Aphrodite's Child.
His Chariots of Fire score won the Academy Award for Best Original Score.
He recorded several albums with Yes singer Jon Anderson as Jon and Vangelis.

cousins.why: Another composer who moved from pop groups to celebrated synth film scores.
Progressive rock that shares his grand, melodic scale; he worked with its singer.

artists.name: Cabaret Voltaire
artists.summary: A Sheffield trio who used tape loops, cheap synths and cut-up vocals to help create industrial music. They later moved toward dance music and electro-funk.
know: The original lineup was Richard H. Kirk, Stephen Mallinder and Chris Watson.
They ran their own Western Works studio in Sheffield.
Their early records came out on Rough Trade.

influencedBy.why: Their cut-up rhythms and tape experiments took cues from Can.
They took the Velvets' drone and noise into electronic territory.
Kraftwerk showed them what a band built on machines could be.
Eno's tape and studio treatments shaped their early methods.

cousins.why: Minimal machines and confrontational atmosphere in early post-punk.
Post-punk built on dub space and abrasive texture.

artists.name: The Human League
artists.summary: A Sheffield band who went from stark experimental electronics to the polished synth-pop of Dare. Don't You Want Me made them international stars.
know: After founders Martyn Ware and Ian Craig Marsh left in 1980 to form Heaven 17, Phil Oakey recruited Joanne Catherall and Susan Ann Sulley.
Dare was produced by Martin Rushent and topped the UK chart.
Their 1986 US number one Human was written and produced by Jimmy Jam and Terry Lewis.

influencedBy.why: Their all-synthesizer approach followed Kraftwerk's lead.
Moroder's electronic disco shaped their sound, and Oakey later recorded Together in Electric Dreams with him.
Roxy Music's art-pop styling was an early model.
Jam and Lewis produced the Crash album and wrote Human.
No. 1 in Heaven helped point British bands toward synth-pop.

cousins.why: Early-1980s British synth-driven pop.
Synth-pop that crossed over to US radio.

artists.name: Gary Numan
artists.summary: A London singer who took synthesizers to the top of the UK charts in 1979, first with Tubeway Army and then solo. His cold, robotic style shaped synth-pop and later industrial rock.
know: Are Friends Electric? by Tubeway Army and his solo single Cars both reached number one in the UK in 1979.
He discovered the Minimoog when one was left in the studio during the Tubeway Army sessions.
His later albums moved toward heavy industrial rock.

influencedBy.why: Bowie's Berlin-era records and persona were a direct model.
Kraftwerk's machine aesthetic shaped his sound.

cousins.why: New wave that made machines and detachment part of the act.
Synth-flavored new wave rock with a cool, clipped delivery.

artists.name: Orchestral Manoeuvres in the Dark
artists.summary: A Wirral duo, Andy McCluskey and Paul Humphreys, who made melodic, often experimental synth-pop. Enola Gay and the Architecture & Morality singles were major European hits.
know: Their first single Electricity came out on Factory Records in 1979, produced by Martin Hannett.
Architecture & Morality used Mellotron choir sounds on Joan of Arc and Maid of Orleans.
If You Leave was written for the film Pretty in Pink and became their biggest US hit.

influencedBy.why: McCluskey and Humphreys have said hearing Kraftwerk made them start the band.
They have named Neu! as a key influence on their early sound.
Hannett produced their debut single Electricity.

cousins.why: Synth-pop with serious themes and big melodies.
Northern English electronic pop that started on Factory Records.

artists.name: Larry Levan
artists.summary: The resident DJ at New York's Paradise Garage, where his long, dub-heavy sets shaped dance music. The garage style is named after the club, and his remixes are still standards.
know: He played at the Paradise Garage from 1977 until it closed in 1987.
He and Frankie Knuckles came up together, both working at the Continental Baths.
He produced and mixed the Peech Boys' Don't Make Me Wait.
songs: Is It All Over My Face (Loose Joints)
I Got My Mind Made Up (Instant Funk)

influencedBy.why: They learned to DJ side by side as teenagers in New York.
Love Is the Message became a staple of Levan's sets at the Paradise Garage.

cousins.why: A mixer who treated the mixing desk as an instrument, as Levan did with dub disco.
A DJ whose sets at one venue created a new genre.

artists.name: Marshall Jefferson
artists.summary: A Chicago producer whose Move Your Body helped define house music in 1986. He also produced Phuture's Acid Tracks and early records by Ten City.
know: Move Your Body was one of the first house records to use piano, and became known as the house music anthem.
He was working at the post office when he started making tracks.
He produced Ce Ce Rogers's Someday and Ten City's Foundation.

influencedBy.why: Vocal garage-style house from Chicago drew on the sound Levan made famous.
Hearing Knuckles DJ in Chicago drew him into house music.

cousins.why: A drum machine and sampler pioneer in New York hip hop in the same years.
A producer who built a new dance genre from machines and gospel-rooted vocals.

artists.name: Larry Heard
artists.summary: A Chicago producer, also known as Mr. Fingers, who brought jazz chords and warmth to house music. Can You Feel It is a founding record of deep house.
know: He played drums in jazz and funk bands before making house tracks.
He formed Fingers Inc. with singers Robert Owens and Ron Wilson.
He made Can You Feel It on a Roland Juno-60 synth.

influencedBy.why: His jazz-fusion chords and synth tones carry the sound of Hancock's 1970s records.

cousins.why: A jazz pianist known for soft, rich chords and mood.
Smooth, late-night soul that shares his warmth and restraint.

artists.name: Phuture
artists.summary: A Chicago trio whose 1987 record Acid Tracks created acid house. They found the squelching sound by twisting the knobs of a Roland TB-303 bass machine.
know: The group was DJ Pierre, Earl Spanky Smith Jr. and Herb J.
DJ Ron Hardy played their tape at the Music Box club before it was released.
Acid Tracks came out on Trax Records in 1987.

influencedBy.why: He produced Acid Tracks and helped bring it to Trax Records.

cousins.why: A record that found a new genre in a Roland drum machine.
Minimal machine music with a raw, hypnotic edge.

artists.name: Derrick May
artists.summary: One of the Belleville Three who created Detroit techno. Strings of Life, released as Rhythim Is Rhythm, is one of the genre's defining records.

He released his music as Rhythim Is Rhythm on his own Transmat label.
The piano part of Strings of Life was played by Michael James.

influencedBy.why: Atkins was his friend and mentor and taught him to make music with machines.
Kraftwerk's records were central to the Belleville Three's sound.
Moroder's electronic disco was part of the music they grew up on.
Detroit's love of P-Funk fed the futurist side of his music.

cousins.why: Jazz-rooted electronic music with a futurist edge.
Machine funk that started a new genre in the 1980s.

artists.name: Kevin Saunderson
artists.summary: The Belleville Three member who took Detroit techno to the pop charts with Inner City. His Reese bass sound became a building block of drum and bass.

His track Just Want Another Chance, released as Reese, gave its name to the Reese bass sound.
He runs the KMS label.

influencedBy.why: Atkins was a friend and mentor in Belleville.
May was his school friend and fellow founder of the scene.
Kraftwerk shaped the electronic sound they built on.

cousins.why: Dance music with big crossover pop hooks.
House music that crossed into mainstream success.

artists.name: Jeff Mills
artists.summary: A Detroit DJ and producer known for fast, minimal techno and very fast three-deck DJ sets. He co-founded Underground Resistance and later scored films and played with orchestras.

He co-founded Underground Resistance with Mike Banks.
He started the Axis label in 1992.

influencedBy.why: Atkins's early Detroit techno set the ground he built on.
Kraftwerk's precise machine music is a stated reference.
He and Mills recorded together, including the 2018 EP Tomorrow Comes the Harvest.

cousins.why: A musician who built his work around space and the future.
The Afrobeat drummer recorded an album with Mills in 2018.

artists.name: Underground Resistance
artists.summary: A Detroit techno collective founded by Mike Banks and Jeff Mills with a strong independent and political stance. They kept their faces hidden and built their own distribution.

Members often appeared in masks to keep the focus on the music.

influencedBy.why: Their sci-fi funk mythology is a clear model.
Atkins's Detroit techno was the base they built on.
They took Public Enemy's militant, message-driven stance into techno.

cousins.why: A band that ran its own business on independent principles.
Afrofuturist music with its own mythology.

artists.name: Carl Craig
artists.summary: A second-wave Detroit techno producer who brought jazz and experiment into the music. His Planet E label and many aliases made him one of techno's most varied artists.

He founded the Planet E label in 1991.

keyAlbums: More Songs About Food and Revolutionary Art

influencedBy.why: May mentored Craig and released his early tracks on Transmat.
Atkins's early Detroit techno shaped his starting point.
Kraftwerk's records are part of every Detroit producer's foundation.

cousins.why: Jazz that moves easily into electronic production.
Jazz and machine music meeting in one artist.

artists.name: Drexciya
artists.summary: A secretive Detroit electro duo who built a whole underwater science-fiction mythology around their records. Their cold, aquatic electro is a cornerstone of Afrofuturist dance music.

Their track and album titles describe an undersea civilisation called Drexciya.
James Stinson died in 2002, the year Harnessed the Storm and Grava 4 came out.

influencedBy.why: Drexciya released early records through the UR camp and its distributor.
Kraftwerk's electro foundations run through their sound.
Planet Rock's electro template is the base of their style.
P-Funk's sci-fi mythology shaped their storytelling.

cousins.why: Afrofuturist music with its own cosmic mythology.
A masked artist who built a full fictional world around the music.

artists.name: Richie Hawtin
artists.summary: A producer and DJ from Windsor, across the river from Detroit, best known as Plastikman. His stripped-back acid and minimal records shaped 1990s techno.
