know: Nigel Godrich produced The Man Who.
Oasis gave them support slots on tour.
Why Does It Always Rain on Me? became their signature song.
songs: Why Does It Always Rain on Me?

influencedBy.why: Produced The Man Who and The Invisible Band.
They supported Oasis, and Writing to Reach You borrows Wonderwall's chords.
Their melodic songwriting follows the Beatles.
Their gentle guitar ballads follow Radiohead.

cousins.why: Glasgow guitar pop.
Gentle, melodic songwriting.

artists.name: Placebo
artists.summary: London band led by Brian Molko, known for dark, androgynous glam rock. David Bowie championed them and recorded with them.
know: David Bowie recorded a version of Without You I'm Nothing with them.
They covered Kate Bush's Running Up That Hill.
Their debut album came out in 1996.

influencedBy.why: Bowie championed them and recorded with them.
Molko has named Sonic Youth as an influence.
Their dark, moody sound follows the Cure.
They covered Running Up That Hill.
Their loud-quiet dynamics follow the Pixies.

cousins.why: Dark, moody rock.
Dark, moody alternative.

artists.name: Stereophonics
artists.summary: Welsh band fronted by Kelly Jones, known for his raspy voice and songs about small-town life.
know: They were the first band signed to Richard Branson's V2 label.
Dakota was their first UK number-one single.
The band came from the village of Cwmaman in the Welsh valleys.

influencedBy.why: Kelly Jones has named Rod Stewart as a vocal influence.
Their loose rock follows the Faces.
Their Britpop follows Oasis.

cousins.why: Raspy-voiced rock.
Raspy, soulful vocals.

artists.name: Kasabian
artists.summary: Leicester band led by Serge Pizzorno that mixed swaggering guitar rock with electronic beats. They became one of the biggest British rock bands of the 2000s.
know: Dan the Automator produced West Ryder Pauper Lunatic Asylum.
Club Foot was their breakthrough single.
They headlined Glastonbury in 2014.

influencedBy.why: Their mix of rock and dance follows Primal Scream.
Their swaggering guitar rock follows the Stone Roses.
Their dance grooves follow the Happy Mondays.
Their electronic beats follow the Chemical Brothers.
Their big British rock choruses follow Oasis.

cousins.why: Rock energy with electronic beats.
Rock mixed with beats.

artists.name: Big Bill Broonzy
artists.summary: A prolific Chicago guitarist and songwriter who helped turn rural blues into a city sound, then carried the blues to folk audiences in the US and Europe.
know: He recorded hundreds of sides in the 1930s and 1940s and was a central figure in the Bluebird label's Chicago scene.
He wrote or popularized "Key to the Highway," later recorded by Little Walter, Eric Clapton and Derek and the Dominos.
His 1950s tours of Britain introduced many young musicians there to live acoustic blues.
keyAlbums: Big Bill Broonzy Sings Folk Songs

influencedBy.why: His early fingerpicked country blues follows the Texas style Jefferson made popular on record.
Broonzy's urban blues of the 1930s followed Carr's smoother model.
Johnson's clean single-note guitar lines are part of the vocabulary Broonzy brought into his playing.

cousins.why: A traveling songwriter who bridged rural roots music and the folk revival in the same way.
Another early star who blended blues and folk songs into a personal, widely copied style.

artists.name: Memphis Minnie
artists.summary: A guitarist, singer and songwriter who was one of the most successful blues artists of the 1930s and an early electric guitar player in Chicago.
know: She recorded "When the Levee Breaks" in 1929 with her partner Kansas Joe McCoy.
She recorded around 200 songs over three decades, an unusually long run for a blues artist of her era.
She was playing electric guitar in Chicago clubs by the early 1940s.

influencedBy.why: She came up in the same Mississippi Delta circuit where Patton's rough, rhythmic guitar was the model.
Rainey's touring blues shows set the template for a woman leading her own blues act.
Jefferson's records spread the guitar-led blues style she built on.

cousins.why: Maybelle Carter was a similarly influential early woman guitarist in country music.
A self-taught woman guitarist whose distinctive picking shaped later folk players.

artists.name: Thomas A. Dorsey
artists.summary: A blues pianist who became the father of modern gospel music, writing hundreds of songs and building the organizations that spread them.
know: As "Georgia Tom" he led Ma Rainey's band and recorded the hit "It's Tight Like That" with Tampa Red in 1928.
He wrote "Take My Hand, Precious Lord" in 1932, which became one of the most recorded gospel songs.
He co-founded the National Convention of Gospel Choirs and Choruses in 1933.
keyAlbums: Precious Lord: New Recordings of the Great Gospel Songs of Thomas A. Dorsey

influencedBy.why: He worked as Rainey's pianist and bandleader, learning blues showmanship firsthand.
His recording partnership with Tampa Red shaped the hokum style he played before turning to gospel.
Handy's published blues set the pattern for a songwriter selling blues as sheet music, which Dorsey later did for gospel.

cousins.why: A songwriter whose catalog defined what a whole genre sang for decades.
Sacred songs set to popular music in a different tradition.

artists.name: Tampa Red
artists.summary: Billed as "The Guitar Wizard," he brought a clean, precise slide style to city blues and wrote songs that became blues standards.
know: He played a gold-plated National resonator guitar that became his trademark.
He wrote "It Hurts Me Too" and "Black Angel Blues," later recast by Elmore James and B.B. King.
His Chicago home served as a rehearsal space and boarding house for many Bluebird label musicians.

influencedBy.why: His duo with Dorsey produced the hokum hits that launched his career.
Johnson's clean single-string phrasing is close to Tampa Red's precise approach.
Jefferson's records set the early model for a solo blues guitarist on record.

cousins.why: A guitar virtuoso of the same era who made his instrument a lead voice.
Western swing's steel guitar sound shares the singing, sliding lead line.

artists.name: Leroy Carr
artists.summary: A pianist and singer whose relaxed, city style and duets with guitarist Scrapper Blackwell made him one of the best-selling blues artists of the early 1930s.
know: His first record, "How Long, How Long Blues" in 1928, was a major hit.
His partnership with guitarist Scrapper Blackwell made the piano and guitar duo a standard blues format.
His calm, conversational singing contrasted with the shouting style common at the time.

influencedBy.why: The classic blues singers like Smith defined the songs and forms he reshaped for a smaller setting.
Rainey's recorded blues were part of the repertoire his generation learned from.
Johnson's smooth, urbane blues records of the mid-1920s pointed toward Carr's own sound.

cousins.why: A pianist-singer known for the same relaxed, conversational delivery.
A crooner who also replaced shouting with an easy, close-to-the-microphone style.

artists.name: Blind Willie Johnson
artists.summary: A street-singing evangelist whose 30 recordings combined a rough false-bass voice with slide guitar and became cornerstones of gospel blues.
know: He recorded all of his known music, 30 sides, for Columbia between 1927 and 1930.
His instrumental "Dark Was the Night, Cold Was the Ground" was included on the Voyager Golden Record in 1977.
He sang in a deliberately gravelly low voice and often traded lines with a female singer.
songs: Dark Was the Night, Cold Was the Ground
Jesus Make Up My Dying Bed

influencedBy.why: Jefferson was the leading Texas guitarist on record when Johnson began, and Johnson worked the same street circuit.

cousins.why: Hypnotic, spiritual guitar music rooted in an older tradition.
Stark sacred singing with the same haunted intensity.

artists.name: Blind Willie McTell
artists.summary: An Atlanta twelve-string guitarist with a smooth voice and ragtime-flavored picking whose "Statesboro Blues" became a rock standard.
know: He recorded under several names, including Blind Sammie and Georgia Bill, for different labels.
John Lomax recorded him for the Library of Congress in 1940, including spoken memories of his career.
Bob Dylan wrote a song titled "Blind Willie McTell" in his honor in 1983.

influencedBy.why: Jefferson's hit records set the model for a blind street guitarist making records in the 1920s.

cousins.why: A fingerpicking guitarist who kept old songs alive with clean, rhythmic playing.
A folk guitarist known for intricate, ragtime-tinged picking.

artists.name: Lonnie Johnson
artists.summary: A guitarist and singer who pioneered the single-note guitar solo and moved easily between blues, jazz and ballads over a 45-year career.
know: He recorded with Louis Armstrong's Hot Five and Duke Ellington's orchestra in the late 1920s.
His 1929 guitar duets with Eddie Lang are among the first great jazz guitar records.
His ballad "Tomorrow Night" was a number one R&B hit in 1948.

influencedBy.why: Recording with Armstrong's Hot Five put him at the center of the new soloist-driven jazz.
He played on Ellington records in 1928, blending blues guitar with orchestral jazz.
He came up in the New Orleans music world that Oliver's bands defined.

cousins.why: A guitarist of the same era who turned the guitar into a solo voice.
A guitarist whose distinctive technique set a template for an entire genre.

artists.name: Mamie Smith
artists.summary: A vaudeville singer whose 1920 record "Crazy Blues" was the first blues vocal recording by an African American singer and proved a market for Black music on record.
know: "Crazy Blues," written by Perry Bradford, sold strongly within months of its 1920 release.
Her success led labels to create "race records" series aimed at Black audiences.
Her backing band, the Jazz Hounds, included a young Coleman Hawkins.
songs: You Can't Keep a Good Man Down

influencedBy.why: Handy's published blues gave vaudeville singers like Smith a ready blues repertoire.

cousins.why: Another first record that proved a new genre could sell.
A vaudeville star who became one of the first big names on record.

artists.name: W.C. Handy
artists.summary: A bandleader, composer and publisher known as the Father of the Blues, who wrote down and published blues songs that became standards.
know: He published "The Memphis Blues" in 1912 and "St. Louis Blues" in 1914.
He described hearing a guitarist play slide with a knife at a Mississippi train station in 1903 as his first encounter with the blues.
He co-founded a music publishing company with Harry Pace that issued his songs.
keyAlbums: Louis Armstrong Plays W.C. Handy (Louis Armstrong)

influencedBy.why: Handy's composed blues grew out of the same written ragtime tradition Joplin led.

cousins.why: A composer who wrote down and published a vernacular style.
A songwriter-publisher whose catalog became standard repertoire.

artists.name: Tommy Johnson
artists.summary: A Delta singer and guitarist whose eerie falsetto and handful of 1928 to 1929 recordings made him one of the most copied bluesmen of his region.
know: He learned in the Drew, Mississippi area where Charley Patton and Willie Brown played.
He recorded for Victor in 1928 and Paramount in 1929, leaving only a small body of work.
The band Canned Heat took its name from his "Canned Heat Blues."

influencedBy.why: He learned his craft in the Patton circle around Drew and shared much of Patton's rhythmic approach.

cousins.why: A rural 1920s recording artist with a few haunting sides and an outsized legacy.
High lonesome singing with the same eerie upper register.

artists.name: Mississippi Sheiks
artists.summary: A fiddle and guitar string band led by Walter Vinson and Lonnie Chatmon whose 1930 hit "Sitting on Top of the World" became a standard in blues, country and rock.
know: The group was built around members of the musical Chatmon family.
They played dances for both Black and white audiences, mixing blues with popular and country tunes.
"Sitting on Top of the World" was later recorded by Bob Wills, Howlin' Wolf, Cream and the Grateful Dead.
songs: Sitting on Top of the World

influencedBy.why: They came out of the same Delta dance music world that Patton dominated.

cousins.why: A family string act whose recordings became standards across genres.
A modern string band playing old-time dance music with the same drive.

artists.name: Sonny Boy Williamson I
artists.summary: John Lee Williamson was the first great blues harmonica star on record, making the harp a lead instrument in Chicago band blues.
know: His 1937 Bluebird single "Good Morning, School Girl" became one of the most covered blues songs.
He recorded more than 120 sides for Bluebird and RCA Victor.
Rice Miller later performed under the same name, which is why the two are numbered I and II.

influencedBy.why: Williamson was part of the Bluebird circle that rehearsed and recorded around Tampa Red.
He worked in the Bluebird Chicago circle where Broonzy was a leading figure and session player.

cousins.why: A harmonica player whose harp became part of his musical identity.
Made the harmonica a lead voice in soul and pop.

artists.name: Sonny Boy Williamson II
artists.summary: Aleck "Rice" Miller was a harmonica player and witty songwriter who hosted the King Biscuit Time radio show and later recorded classic Chess sides.
know: He hosted KFFA's King Biscuit Time radio show in Helena starting in 1941.
He recorded for Trumpet Records and then for Chess's Checker label from 1955.
On his 1963 and 1964 European tours he recorded with the Yardbirds and the Animals.
keyAlbums: Sonny Boy Williamson and the Yardbirds

influencedBy.why: Rice Miller took his name and expanded on his style.
He performed alongside Robert Johnson in the Delta in the 1930s.
James's "Dust My Broom" was cut at one of Miller's Trumpet sessions, with Miller on harmonica.
Dixon played bass on and helped shape his Chess recordings.
Chess's Checker label recorded his classic sides.

cousins.why: A harmonica-playing songwriter known for sly, wordy storytelling.
A harmonica-wielding singer who stretched the blues in odd directions.

artists.name: Big Joe Turner
artists.summary: A powerful Kansas City blues shouter whose 1950s Atlantic records, led by "Shake, Rattle and Roll," were a direct bridge to rock and roll.
know: He started as a singing bartender in Kansas City, working with boogie-woogie pianist Pete Johnson.
Turner and Johnson performed "Roll 'Em Pete" at the From Spirituals to Swing concert at Carnegie Hall in 1938.
His 1954 "Shake, Rattle and Roll" was covered the same year by Bill Haley and in 1956 by Elvis Presley.

influencedBy.why: Signed Turner and produced Shake, Rattle and Roll.
He came up in the same Kansas City jam session scene as Basie's band.
The big-voiced classic blues singers set the model for his shouting delivery.

cousins.why: A rock and roll shouter with the same force.
A soul shouter who drove a band with sheer vocal power.

artists.name: Lightnin' Hopkins
artists.summary: A Houston guitarist and singer with a loose, improvised style who recorded prolifically for decades and became a hero of the folk blues revival.
know: As a boy he met Blind Lemon Jefferson and later toured with his cousin, singer Texas Alexander.
He got his nickname at a 1946 Aladdin Records session alongside pianist Wilson "Thunder" Smith.
He is thought to have recorded more albums than almost any other blues musician.

influencedBy.why: He met and played for Jefferson as a child and modeled his early guitar on Jefferson's Texas style.

cousins.why: A storyteller who made up verses on the spot about his own life.
A gravel-voiced storyteller with the same loose, lived-in feel.

artists.name: Wynonie Harris
artists.summary: A flamboyant blues shouter whose late-1940s King Records hits, especially "Good Rockin' Tonight," helped set the stage for rock and roll.
know: He first scored with Lucky Millinder's band on "Who Threw the Whiskey in the Well" in 1945.
His 1948 version of Roy Brown's "Good Rockin' Tonight" went to number one on the R&B chart.
His energetic stage act was a model for later rock and roll performers.
songs: Who Threw the Whiskey in the Well
All She Wants to Do Is Rock

influencedBy.why: Harris followed Turner's model of the big-voiced blues shouter in front of a band.
Jordan's jump blues set the small-band style Harris's records used.

cousins.why: A showman whose stage act was as important as his records.
A rock and roll pioneer who also built on jump blues.

artists.name: Roy Brown
artists.summary: A New Orleans singer who wrote "Good Rockin' Tonight" and brought a gospel-style crying vocal to rhythm and blues.
know: He recorded "Good Rockin' Tonight" for DeLuxe Records in 1947.
He started out imitating Bing Crosby before adopting a pleading, gospel-influenced blues style.
"Hard Luck Blues" was a number one R&B hit in 1950.

influencedBy.why: He began singing in Crosby's crooning style before moving to blues.
Turner's blues shouting was the established model Brown modified with a gospel cry.
Jordan's jump blues set the small-band format Brown's records used.

cousins.why: Another singer who brought gospel feeling into secular R&B.
A soul singer with the same pleading, emotional delivery.

artists.name: Big Mama Thornton
artists.summary: A commanding blues singer who made the original hit of "Hound Dog" and wrote "Ball and Chain," two songs that shaped rock and roll and 1960s rock.
know: Her 1953 "Hound Dog," written by Leiber and Stoller and produced by Johnny Otis, was a number one R&B hit.
She wrote "Ball and Chain," which Janis Joplin made famous at Monterey Pop in 1967.
She also played harmonica and drums on stage.

influencedBy.why: Wrote and produced Hound Dog for Thornton.
Thornton named Memphis Minnie among the singers she admired most.
Thornton named Bessie Smith as a model for her powerful voice.
Otis led her band and produced "Hound Dog."

cousins.why: A powerhouse voice in folk with the same commanding presence.
A soul singer with a heavy, blues-rooted voice.

artists.name: Professor Longhair
artists.summary: Henry Roeland Byrd was a New Orleans pianist who mixed boogie-woogie with rumba and calypso rhythms, creating the city's distinctive piano sound.
know: "Tipitina" and "Mardi Gras in New Orleans" are New Orleans anthems.
After years out of music, his 1971 New Orleans Jazz and Heritage Festival appearance revived his career.
His final studio album, Crawfish Fiesta, came out in 1980.

influencedBy.why: Morton's Caribbean "Spanish tinge" in New Orleans piano is the older form of the rhythms Longhair used.

cousins.why: Latin rhythm put at the center of dance music.
Caribbean rhythm mixed with R&B in another port city.

artists.name: Otis Spann
artists.summary: The pianist in Muddy Waters' band for more than 15 years, he defined the role of piano in electric Chicago blues and played on many Chess classics.
know: He joined Muddy Waters' band in 1952 and stayed until 1968.
He played on Chess sessions for Howlin' Wolf, Little Walter, Bo Diddley and others.
He recorded The Biggest Thing Since Colossus in 1969 with members of Fleetwood Mac.
songs: It Must Have Been the Devil

influencedBy.why: As Muddy's longtime pianist he shaped and was shaped by the band's sound.
Dixon ran many of the Chess sessions Spann played on.
He worked with Little Walter in Muddy's band and on Walter's own records.

cousins.why: A keyboard player whose session work defined a label's sound.
A band keyboardist who shaped many classic records from behind the leader.

artists.name: Jimmy Rogers
artists.summary: The second guitarist in Muddy Waters' classic early-1950s band, he also cut his own Chess hits and helped set the two-guitar Chicago sound.
know: He played rhythm guitar in Muddy Waters' band alongside Little Walter from the late 1940s.
His Chess singles included "That's All Right" in 1950 and "Walking by Myself" in 1956.
His last album, Blues Blues Blues, featured Eric Clapton, Mick Jagger, Keith Richards, Jimmy Page and Robert Plant.

influencedBy.why: As Muddy's bandmate he built the interlocking two-guitar band sound.
He played alongside Little Walter in Muddy's band and on early sessions.
He started on harmonica in the Chicago style the first Sonny Boy made popular.

cousins.why: Tight interlocking band playing where every part locks together.
Players whose ensemble feel mattered more than any single solo.

artists.name: Slim Harpo
artists.summary: A Baton Rouge harmonica player and singer whose laid-back Excello records, such as "I'm a King Bee," were widely covered by British Invasion bands.
know: He recorded for Excello with producer J.D. Miller in Crowley, Louisiana.
"Baby Scratch My Back" reached number one on the R&B chart in 1966.
His songs were covered by the Rolling Stones, the Kinks, the Yardbirds and the Doors.
songs: Got Love If You Want It

influencedBy.why: His relaxed vocal and harmonica-on-a-rack approach follows Jimmy Reed's style.
Little Walter's harmonica records set the standard for the instrument in 1950s blues.

cousins.why: Easygoing, groove-first singing in a Caribbean style.
Swampy, Louisiana-flavored rock with the same steady groove.

artists.name: Charles Brown
artists.summary: A pianist and singer whose soft, after-hours style defined West Coast club blues and who wrote two enduring Christmas songs.
know: He sang and played on Johnny Moore's Three Blazers' 1945 hit "Drifting Blues."
He recorded "Merry Christmas Baby" in 1947 and "Please Come Home for Christmas" in 1960.
Before music he earned a college degree in chemistry and worked as a teacher.

influencedBy.why: Brown's soft piano blues carries on Carr's quiet, intimate approach.
Cole's piano trio and gentle vocals were the direct model for Brown's style.

cousins.why: Late-night ballad singing with the same intimate mood.
A cool, smoky, after-hours feel in another era.

artists.name: Leonard Chess
artists.summary: Co-founder with his brother Phil of Chess Records, the Chicago label that recorded Muddy Waters, Howlin' Wolf, Chuck Berry and many more.
know: He and Phil Chess turned their Aristocrat label into Chess Records in 1950.
Chess released "Rocket 88" in 1951, often called one of the first rock and roll records.
He also bought Chicago radio station WVON in 1963.
keyAlbums: The Best of Muddy Waters (Muddy Waters)

influencedBy.why: Muddy was the first major artist Chess recorded, and his success shaped the label.
Dixon was the label's chief writer, bassist and session leader.
Phillips supplied Chess with early masters including "Rocket 88" and Howlin' Wolf.

cousins.why: Built a label whose roster defined a city's sound.
Another 1950s label owner who recorded the roots of rock and roll.

artists.name: The Golden Gate Quartet
artists.summary: A Virginia vocal group whose rhythmic jubilee style, with vocal lines imitating instruments, made them the most popular gospel quartet of the late 1930s and 1940s.
know: They began recording for Bluebird in 1937.
They sang at the From Spirituals to Swing concert at Carnegie Hall in 1938.
The group relocated to France in 1959 and has continued there with changing members.

influencedBy.why: The Mills Brothers' tight harmony and vocal instrument effects were a model for the Gates' rhythmic style.

cousins.why: Intricate vocal harmony as the main instrument.
A vocal group whose rhythmic, sacred harmony carries every song.

artists.name: The Soul Stirrers
artists.summary: A Texas gospel quartet that pioneered the hard gospel lead-singer style and launched Sam Cooke, providing a direct line from gospel to soul music.
know: Lead singer R.H. Harris introduced the falsetto lead and the practice of a second lead singer.
Sam Cooke sang lead from 1950 to 1957 on their Specialty Records sides.
Johnnie Taylor replaced Cooke as lead when Cooke left for pop.
songs: Touch the Hem of His Garment

influencedBy.why: The Soul Stirrers built much of their repertoire on the new gospel songs Dorsey published.
Later quartets like the Soul Stirrers grew out of the jubilee style the Gates popularized before moving to a harder sound.

cousins.why: A vocal group trading leads over rich harmony.
A harmony group known for lead singers passing the melody between them.

artists.name: The Dixie Hummingbirds
artists.summary: A long-running gospel quartet led for decades by Ira Tucker, whose dynamic singing and stagecraft influenced R&B performers.
know: James Davis founded the group in Greenville, South Carolina in 1928.
Ira Tucker joined as lead singer in 1938, and the group later based itself in Philadelphia.
They sang backing vocals on Paul Simon's "Loves Me Like a Rock" in 1973.
songs: Let's Go Out to the Programs

influencedBy.why: The Hummingbirds started in the jubilee quartet mold the Gates defined.

cousins.why: A vocal group known for precise harmony and choreography.
A sacred vocal group that also collaborated with Paul Simon.

artists.name: Clara Ward
artists.summary: Leader of the Ward Singers, she was a major gospel star of the 1950s and a mentor to the young Aretha Franklin.
know: She led the Famous Ward Singers, founded by her mother Gertrude Ward.
Their 1950 "Surely God Is Able" was one of the best-selling gospel records of its time.
She took gospel into secular venues, including the Newport Jazz Festival in 1957.
songs: The Day Is Past and Gone

influencedBy.why: The Ward Singers sang in the Dorsey-led gospel convention world and used his songs.

cousins.why: A soul singer with the same gospel power and showmanship.
A soul group rooted in church singing.

artists.name: The Staple Singers
artists.summary: A family group led by Roebuck "Pops" Staples and featuring Mavis Staples, who moved from gospel to message songs and Stax soul hits.
know: Pops Staples played a tremolo-heavy electric guitar that defined their sound.
They signed to Stax in 1968 and had a number one hit with "I'll Take You There" in 1972.
Their songs were connected to the civil rights movement in the 1960s.

influencedBy.why: Played on I'll Take You There and Respect Yourself.
The Staples came out of the Chicago gospel world that Dorsey organized.
The Staples worked the same gospel circuit and shared the hard gospel feel.
Pops Staples grew up near Dockery Farms and learned guitar watching Charley Patton.
Mayfield wrote and produced the Let's Do It Again soundtrack for them.

cousins.why: A family group whose roots recordings became a genre cornerstone.
A family band mixing gospel feeling with social messages.

artists.name: Cab Calloway
artists.summary: A singer and bandleader famous for "Minnie the Moocher" and its hi-de-ho call and response, who led one of the most popular bands of the swing era.
know: His band followed Duke Ellington's as the house orchestra at the Cotton Club.
His band included Dizzy Gillespie, Chu Berry, Milt Hinton and Cozy Cole at different points.
He published a slang glossary, the Hepster's Dictionary, in 1938.

influencedBy.why: Armstrong's scat singing was the model for Calloway's vocal improvising.
Following Ellington at the Cotton Club set the standard his band worked to match.

cousins.why: A bandleader whose stage energy and call and response defined his act.
A sharp-dressed showband built on comedy and audience interplay.

artists.name: Chick Webb
artists.summary: A drummer and bandleader whose band ruled the Savoy Ballroom and who gave a teenage Ella Fitzgerald her start.
know: His band was the house band at Harlem's Savoy Ballroom and was known for winning battles of the bands.
He hired Ella Fitzgerald in 1935, and they had a hit with "A-Tisket, A-Tasket" in 1938.
"Stompin' at the Savoy" was written by his saxophonist and arranger Edgar Sampson.

influencedBy.why: Henderson's arranged Harlem big band was the model Webb's Savoy band built on.

cousins.why: A drummer who led a dance band from behind his instruments.
A band built to keep a dance floor moving.

artists.name: Fletcher Henderson
artists.summary: A pianist, arranger and bandleader whose Harlem orchestra and arrangements created the basic sound of swing-era big bands.
know: His band hired Louis Armstrong in 1924, bringing the New Orleans soloist style to New York.
With Don Redman he developed the call and response between brass and reed sections used by later big bands.
His arrangements, such as "King Porter Stomp," powered Benny Goodman's band in the mid-1930s.

influencedBy.why: Armstrong's time in his band changed how his musicians soloed and swung.
"Sugar Foot Stomp" is an arrangement of Oliver's "Dippermouth Blues."
His famous "King Porter Stomp" arrangement is built on Morton's tune.

cousins.why: An arranger who shaped the sound of other people's hit records.
An arranger and producer who set a template for a whole era.

artists.name: Sidney Bechet
artists.summary: A New Orleans clarinetist and soprano saxophonist who was one of jazz's first great soloists and later became a star in France.
know: Swiss conductor Ernest Ansermet praised his playing in London in 1919, one of the first serious reviews of a jazz musician.
His 1939 Blue Note recording of "Summertime" was an early hit for the label.
He moved to France in 1950, and "Petite Fleur" became a major hit there.

influencedBy.why: He played in Oliver's band in New Orleans as a young musician.

cousins.why: A star of French popular music in the same postwar years.
A singer whose fame was centered in French-speaking Europe.

artists.name: James P. Johnson
artists.summary: The father of Harlem stride piano, a composer of "The Charleston" and teacher of Fats Waller.
know: His piano rolls of "Carolina Shout" were studied note for note by young pianists, including Duke Ellington.
He wrote "The Charleston" for the 1923 Broadway show Runnin' Wild.
He accompanied Bessie Smith on several of her records.
songs: If I Could Be with You

influencedBy.why: Stride grew directly out of the ragtime that Joplin's compositions defined.

cousins.why: A pianist who created a city's signature piano style.
A pianist who played with a pounding, two-handed drive.

artists.name: Earl Hines
artists.summary: A pianist who freed jazz piano from stride with his horn-like "trumpet style" and whose big band incubated the first generation of bebop.
know: He recorded the duet "Weather Bird" with Louis Armstrong in 1928.
His band was based at Chicago's Grand Terrace Cafe for about 12 years.
His 1943 band included Charlie Parker, Dizzy Gillespie and Sarah Vaughan.
songs: Boogie Woogie on St. Louis Blues

influencedBy.why: Playing with Armstrong led him to phrase the right hand like a trumpet line.
He started from the stride style Johnson defined and broke it open.

cousins.why: A pianist-bandleader whose band shaped the next generation.
A virtuoso pianist who made the piano a showpiece.

artists.name: Glenn Miller
artists.summary: A trombonist and arranger whose orchestra, with its clarinet-led reed sound, was the most popular dance band in America from 1939 to 1942.
know: His signature sound placed a clarinet above four saxophones.

artists.name: Tommy Dorsey

artists.name: Ben Webster

artists.name: Sarah Vaughan
